meta.title: Who really said "Pride goeth before a fall"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not a Bible verse. Proverbs 16:18 (KJV, 1611) reads "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall." The short form truncates it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Pride goeth before a fall'?
meta.ogDescription: The verb is genuinely King James; the sentence is not. In Proverbs 16:18, "goeth" comes before destruction — "a fall" belongs to the next clause.

answer.label: Not a Bible verse — a truncation of Proverbs 16:18
answer.authorName: The Book of Proverbs (King James Version)
answer.authorDates: Proverbs 16:18 · King James Version, first published 1611
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely biblical and the verb is genuinely King James — but the sentence is not scripture. Proverbs 16:18 in the KJV reads in full: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.” The familiar one-liner keeps ‘Pride goeth’ from the first clause and ‘a fall’ from the second, dropping ‘destruction’ and the ‘haughty spirit’ that connects them. No major English translation prints the short form as a verse: it appears in none of the versions Bible Hub lists.

source.heading: The verse behind the half-quote

docMeta.dd: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.”
A truncation — ‘Pride goeth’ from the first clause, ‘a fall’ from the second. Printed in none of the English translations Bible Hub lists.

source.excerpt: The highway of the upright is to depart from evil: he that keepeth his way preserveth his soul. Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall. Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud.
trail: Read the verse in full. The King James text of Proverbs 16 gives verse 18 as “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” — the archaic verb is real, but it precedes ‘destruction,’ not ‘a fall.’
Checked whether any translation shortens it. The parallel-translation table at Bible Hub lists the KJV, ESV and NIV all retaining both clauses; none reads simply “Pride goeth before a fall.”

Checked the proverb’s etymology. Wiktionary’s entry for this exact form defines it only as an alternative form of ‘pride comes before a fall,’ whose main entry gives the etymology “Probably a truncation of Proverbs 16:18” and quotes the 1611 printing as “Pride goeth before destruction: and an hautie spirit before a fall.”

Checked the phrase historians. Phrase Finder states that “neither version is exactly as the proverb was originally written,” tracing the line to Proverbs 16:18 and quoting Wycliffe’s Bible of 1382 and the Coverdale Bible of 1535. Quote Investigator has no article on this phrase, and Wikiquote carries no sourced or misattributed entry for it.
source.excerptNote: Verse 18 is a two-part parallelism, and the surrounding verses frame it as a lesson in humility. The popular one-liner takes the subject and verb of the first half and the object of the second, discarding ‘destruction’ and the ‘haughty spirit’ that link them.

source.rightsNote: The source text is Proverbs 16:18 in the King James Version, first published in 1611 and long in the public domain in the United States. The shortened proverb is an anonymous folk form with no identifiable author, and the wordings it descends from — Wycliffe 1382, Coverdale 1535, the 1611 KJV — all pre-date 1931 by centuries, so nothing here carries a live copyright in the United States. One curiosity of provenance: the KJV translation is not free everywhere — Wikipedia records its copyright status as perpetually copyrighted in the United Kingdom, where it is published under royal letters patent, and de facto public domain elsewhere.

author.name: The Book of Proverbs
author.heading: Where the idea actually comes from
author.metaLine: Book of the Hebrew Bible · wisdom literature traditionally ascribed to King Solomon
author.bio: The Book of Proverbs is a collection of Hebrew wisdom sayings in the Old Testament. Wikipedia describes it as traditionally ascribed to King Solomon and his students, while noting that it is in scholarly terms a “collection of collections” assembled over a long period, with its superscriptions serving to categorise content rather than to attribute authorship. Its characteristic form is the two-part couplet — a statement answered by a parallel statement — and Proverbs 16:18 is exactly that: pride → destruction, answered by haughty spirit → a fall. That structure is precisely what everyday speech tends to collapse, which is how the half-verse everyone quotes came to exist.

misattribution.heading: It sounds like a verse because it borrows the Bible’s verb
misattribution.intro: People quote “Pride goeth before a fall” as chapter and verse, often with the archaic ‘goeth’ offered as proof. The idea is scriptural; the sentence is not.

items.why: None of the standard English translations prints it. The King James text of Proverbs 16:18 reads “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall,” and the parallel-translation table at Bible Hub shows the KJV, ESV and NIV all keeping both clauses — and no listed version reading simply “Pride goeth before a fall.” (Some modern paraphrases do condense the verse: the Contemporary English Version reduces it to “Too much pride will destroy you.”)

‘Goeth’ is authentic KJV vocabulary, which is why this variant feels the most scriptural of the three. But in the verse it governs ‘destruction’ — pride goeth before destruction. ‘A fall’ belongs to the second clause, where the subject is the haughty spirit (KJV, Proverbs 16).

Wiktionary lists ‘pride goeth before a fall’ as an alternative form of the proverb whose etymology it gives as “Probably a truncation of Proverbs 16:18” (Wiktionary). Phrase Finder puts it plainly: “neither version is exactly as the proverb was originally written” (Phrase Finder).

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine text is Proverbs 16:18 in the King James Version — “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” — as printed in the KJV text of Proverbs.

context.heading: Why this version fools people most
lead: Of the several folk forms of this proverb — ‘goes before a fall,’ ‘comes before a fall,’ ‘goeth before a fall’ — the ‘goeth’ version is the one that sounds unanswerably scriptural, because ‘goeth’ really is the King James verb. The trick is that in the actual verse it governs the wrong noun: pride goeth before destruction. ‘A fall’ is what the second half of the couplet gives to the haughty spirit.

Proverbs is built from tight two-part parallelisms, and repetition wears them down to their most vivid halves. Here the memorable pairing is ‘pride’ and ‘a fall,’ so the connective terms fell away and the archaic verb stayed behind — leaving a sentence that carries the cadence and authority of the King James Bible without appearing in it.
detailsBody: The wording has been in motion for a long time. Phrase Finder quotes Wycliffe’s Bible of 1382 rendering the verse “Pride goth befor contricioun, & befor falling the spirit shall ben enhauncid,” and the Coverdale Bible of 1535 at Proverbs 29:23 reading “After pryde commeth a fall, but a lowly sprete bryngeth greate worshipe” — a separate verse that nonetheless supplied the ‘pride…a fall’ pairing in plain English.

For the modern short form, Phrase Finder’s Gary Martin reports the earliest citation he could find of “pride comes before a fall” in John Gill’s An Exposition of the Old Testament, 1810, and adds that the expression was probably current before then. That is his finding for the ‘comes’ variant specifically; no comparable first-print date is documented for the ‘goeth before a fall’ form, and none is claimed here.
Grammarist describes the same drift — the King James ‘goeth’ wording morphing into ‘pride goes before a fall’ and then ‘pride comes before a fall’ — and notes all three are in current use.
context.pull: Half of one clause, half of the next, and an archaic verb doing the work of a citation.

schema.verdictNote: The text quoted here is genuine scripture — Proverbs 16:18 in the King James Version (1611). What is misattributed is the short form “Pride goeth before a fall” (alternateName), which is quoted as a verse but is a truncation of it and appears in none of the standard English translations.

sourcesVerified.claim: KJV Proverbs 16:18 reads "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall"; verses 17 and 19 read as quoted in the excerpt.

The KJV, ESV and NIV all retain both clauses of Proverbs 16:18; no listed English translation reads simply "Pride goeth before a fall." Not every listed version keeps both clauses, however: the Contemporary English Version condenses the verse to "Too much pride will destroy you."

The page states "neither version is exactly as the proverb was originally written," traces the line to Proverbs 16:18, quotes Wycliffe's Bible 1382 and the Coverdale Bible 1535 at Proverbs 29:23, and names John Gill's An Exposition of the Old Testament, 1810, as the earliest citation the author could find of the "pride comes before a fall" form.

Etymology reads "Probably a truncation of Proverbs 16:18"; the references quote the 1611 King James printing as "Pride goeth before destruction: and an hautie spirit before a fall"; alternative forms listed include "pride goeth before a fall."
The Wiktionary entry for "pride goeth before a fall" defines it only as an alternative form of "pride comes before a fall" and carries no separate etymology or citations.
The proverb originates in Proverbs 16:18 (KJV) and the wording evolved from the "goeth" form to "pride goes before a fall" and then "pride comes before a fall," with all three in current use.
The Book of Proverbs is traditionally ascribed to King Solomon and his students, is described as a "collection of collections," and is built substantially from short parallel sayings.
The King James Version was commissioned in 1604 and first published in 1611; the article's infobox records its copyright status as "Perpetually copyrighted in UK / De facto public domain elsewhere."
